title: For a Price
mood: The first weeks, alone. Then Vexana needs something only one classmate sells, and Selena names her price.

hero.alt: In the dark, Vexana looks down with wet violet eyes, her hair gone pale lavender, two dark horns rising behind her head and star-shaped blades glowing at her shoulders.
hero.credit: Official Guinevere and Vexana comic, page 44

segs.t: The first order took Vexana out of the void onto the dead ground. She stood there all night, staff in hand, and watched the edge of the dome. Nothing came out of it, and nothing went near it. When the sky behind the shell began to pale, a door opened at her back, and she stepped into the dark.
More orders followed, each a place and a time, never a reason.
Enders crossed the void in long silent lines. She moved as they did: she leaned toward where she meant to go, and the void took her there.
One fold of the dark no line ever crossed. She went to see why. Nothing was there, so she stayed.

In that hollow the plates of her armor loosened when she willed it. She drew her school clothes out from under them: the short black jacket, the white blouse, the black vest, the purple skirt. The tie was still knotted from the morning of the corridor.
In the Will’s future she had worn these on her knees in the dust.

She smoothed each fold flat with two fingers, slowly, the way her father had pressed a bent bracket straight. She let go, and they stayed where she had put them. The pink-haired keychain went on top. The plates closed again.
The void slowed her body. She was rarely hungry, and slept little. When she did sleep, she curled beside the folded clothes.
Far off, Enders lay in rows, still as stones. Farther still, the violet glow of the rows stopped at the edge of something vast. Nothing lit it. It never moved.
The Mother Matrix,
she thought.
The Will’s body, if Chang’e’s readings are right.
She never went near it.
And there was the crack.
It hung in the dark, shaped like a four-pointed star. Through it showed night sky over black water, with lights along the shore: the bay below the Academy.
It was the gateway: a door the Enders were widening between their dark and her world. From this side it looked like torn sky.
Each time she looked, it was a little wider. She measured it against her thumb at arm’s length. One day it would be wide enough for that vast thing to pass. It was her clock.
The next order came out of the cold point under her breastbone, the Will’s mark. “The ruins east of the dome. Tonight.”

A door opened where the order said, and gray Enders came through it with her. They tore girders out of fallen houses and dragged the shells of dead Enders out of the weeds, and carried it all back through the door.
To herself she called them feeders: Enders that carried metal home. She did not know where the metal went. While they worked, she ate from cans in dead kitchens and drank from a cistern.

That night they found an Aspirant suit half buried in a ditch, scorched black, one arm gone. It was empty. Its shoulder plate was stamped S·L·K. Someone from the Academy had fought out here and never come back.
Two feeders hauled it out by the legs.
Vexana’s hand came up. Then she let it fall.
I can’t call them off. And an Ender wouldn’t try.
She made herself watch until the door took it.

Often the order was the first one: “The edge of the dome. Before dawn.” She stood on dead shore well outside the shell, where no lamp reached, and watched the bay. The water was empty under an empty sky. She knew what hung behind it.
It has so many eyes,
she thought.
Why does it need mine?
Every place it sent her was empty, and none lay inside the dome, where the Academy’s cameras watched every ward. It kept her from people. She did not know why, and was glad of it.

In the hollow, where no Ender came, she trained. Her wings opened violet and lit the hollow around her. The great arrow came down from above at her call. She held a charged shot in the staff until her arms shook, then let it go.
Then she woke the black orb.
“Dark night, swallow all things,” she said.
The orb drank the light of her wings until nothing showed. She loosed it, and the blast rolled out across the void without a sound.
Between errands she searched the dark for the Control Core, the thing Chang’e said they must destroy to defeat the Will. She found more dark.
One errand took her past the ruined tower where the way home had opened. She climbed it, stair by broken stair, to the top.
Across the city, under the Academy’s beam, lay the girls’ wing. One window was lit, long past midnight.
This late, she knew whose it was. Only one girl in that wing would still be up.
Inside her sleeve the star made no sound.
On the rooftop where Guinevere gave it to her, she had walked to the rail and back five times with a straight face, to hear how far it could beep. “Stop that,” Guinevere had said, delighted.
Now the whole city lay between them.
Over the dead ground the sky was thick with stars. She looked up at them for a long time.
“Without her, even the stars of the night sky lose their shine,” she said.
She looked back down at the window and did not look up again.
Much later it went dark. She waited ten minutes more, in case it lit again.
Far out in the dead ground the feeders were still working. They went wherever the cold point sent them.
If it ever sends us against that wing,
she thought,
I want something in that fight that answers to me.
The door opened behind her.
In the hollow she thought it through, the way she planned a shot. When the Mother Matrix came through and opened its chest to fire, she had to be up there, alive.
Her wings could lift her. But every beat of them spent power she meant to pour into that open core.
She needed armor, and something to carry her up.
Every Aspirant suit had begun as Ender wreckage. Belief had woken it. She had the belief. She needed wreckage the feeders did not carry off.
Every student in her year knew who sold it: Selena, at the crews’ yard outside the outer fence, after dark.
The next feeder run was in the dead ground a long walk out from the dome. Vexana left the feeders stripping a fallen depot and walked in alone.
If they are its eyes,
she thought,
let them watch a depot.
The crews’ yard lay far down the fence from any gate. By day salvage crews sorted their finds there. Only one lamp still burned, swinging over a trestle table under a tarp.
A big man stood at the table, shouting over a crate of plating. “Half price, or I take it!”
Selena sat on the crate’s lid with a lollipop in her cheek. Her Academy jacket hung open, a salvage pass clipped to its pocket. “It’s not half price.”
He swung. She leaned, and the fist missed her ear. He swung again and hit the post. Selena was never where the fists landed.
At last he pinned a hand beside her head and grinned. “Nowhere left to lean.”
“If you get too smug, you’ll get tripped up,” Selena told him.
He lunged. Selena’s heel hooked the tarp rope and pulled it taut. His boot caught it, and he went down in the mud. He got up swearing and stamped off toward the gate.
When his steps were gone, Vexana walked out of the dark into the lamplight.
Selena looked her over, boots to hair. The lollipop moved to her other cheek.
“Nice hair.”
A classmate in Ender plate stood in her lamplight, and Selena had only moved her lollipop. That calm nagged at Vexana for one moment.
A dealer’s nerve,
she decided.
She asks nothing about me. I’ll ask nothing about where her plating comes from.
“I need plating for a full suit,” said Vexana. “Joints. A frame.”
“Sure. It all comes in anyone’s size.”
“You said that in class. ‘For a price.’”
“I did.” Selena tipped her head. “I’d take stipend money. But Missing people don’t draw a stipend.”
Missing. So that was the word for her now.
“What else have you got?” asked Selena.
“Places.” Every feeder run showed her more wreckage than the feeders could carry. “I know where it lies. Before the crews do.”
“Such as?”
“Two dead Enders in the railroad cut north of the old bridge. Whole.”
“Whole?”
“Whole.”
A slow smile. “Deal.”
Selena slid off the crate and sorted plates into a sack. She talked while she sorted, the way people talk about rain.
“Most of them think you’re dead.” She weighed a knee joint in her hand and dropped it in.
“Your partner doesn’t.” Selena looked up from the sack.
Vexana’s face did not move.
She saw the window again, lit long past midnight.
Her left hand started toward her right sleeve. She stopped it halfway.
She’s still waiting up,
she thought.
Then I keep the whole city between us.
Selena went back to sorting. A plate clinked into the sack.
“Genuine Ender plating.” Selena tied off the sack. “The last owner didn’t complain. That’s a knee and a shoulder. Bring me another place, you get the other knee.”
Vexana shouldered the sack. Selena waved the lollipop.
“Ahaha, bye-bye!”
Vexana walked back out to the depot.
Feeders carry scrap,
she thought.
So do I.
When the feeders were done, the door opened for her and the sack alike. It did not care what she carried.
In the hollow she let the sack go beside the folded uniform, and it stayed. On the clothes the pink-haired keychain lay where she had left it, its little face turned toward her.
